title: DNS Transport over TCP - Implementation Requirements
summary: This standards-track RFC requires DNS implementations to support TCP as a transport, not just UDP, and gives guidance for making TCP performance on par with UDP. It obsoletes RFC 5966 and updates RFC 1035 and RFC 1123.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS implementations must support TCP as well as UDP. TCP lets DNS carry complete responses when UDP is not suitable, and the RFC explains how to reuse connections without confusing replies.

questions: when is dns over tcp needed
when does dns fall back to tcp
subtitle: Why DNS implementations must support TCP and how to handle its connections efficiently.

tldr.problem: DNS responses have grown, and UDP truncation or fragmentation can prevent clients from receiving a complete response. Some implementations treated TCP support as optional.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7766 requires general-purpose DNS implementations to support both UDP and TCP. It recommends connection reuse, query pipelining, and handling responses by their message identifiers rather than arrival order.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7766 obsoletes RFC 5966, updates RFC 1035 and RFC 1123, and has since been updated by RFC 8490 and RFC 9103.

facts.label: Recommended connection groups
facts.value: One for regular queries, one for zone transfers, and one per layered protocol

today: RFC 7766 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5966 and updates RFC 1035 and RFC 1123. It has since been updated by RFC 8490 and RFC 9103.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs TCP Support
sections.content:
Most DNS transactions use UDP, but TCP is used for full zone transfers and is often needed for larger messages. DNSSEC and IPv6 have increased response sizes. TCP also provides protection against source-address spoofing that can support reflection and amplification attacks.

RFC 1123 said resolvers and recursive servers SHOULD support TCP for non-zone-transfer queries. Some implementers read that as optional. RFC 7766 updates the core DNS specifications: support for both TCP and UDP is REQUIRED for a full DNS implementation.

The RFC does not set requirements for server operators. It warns that not supporting TCP, or blocking it in a network, will probably cause resolution failures or application timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: Some DNS answers are too large for UDP to carry reliably. Every general-purpose DNS implementation must therefore be able to use TCP too.

sections.title: Why UDP Alone Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Without EDNS0, a DNS server truncates a UDP response that would exceed 512 bytes and sets the TC flag. The client can then retry over TCP. DNSSEC responses have made this truncation common.

EDNS0 lets a client announce that it can receive a larger UDP response. But a UDP packet larger than the path MTU may be fragmented at the IP layer. The RFC notes that firewalls and other network devices often block fragments or cannot reassemble them, and that even responses within a common 1500-byte MTU may be too large.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP can carry only so much data in one response. Larger UDP packets may be split into fragments that some parts of the network cannot deliver or reassemble.

sections.title: Who Must Support Both Transports
sections.content:
All general-purpose DNS implementations MUST support UDP and TCP. Authoritative servers need TCP so they do not limit responses to one UDP packet. Recursive servers and forwarders need it to pass large responses to clients. Stub resolvers need it to interoperate with their upstream servers.

Resolvers are no longer required to send a non-zone-transfer query over UDP first. Stub and recursive resolvers MAY choose TCP or UDP for local operational reasons, and TCP MAY be used before any UDP query. If a TCP connection is already open, a resolver SHOULD reuse it.

Recursive and authoritative servers MUST reply using the same transport as the query. For TCP, the reply MUST use the same connection.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS clients, recursive servers, and authoritative servers all need TCP support. A resolver may choose TCP first, and a server replies using the transport and connection that carried the query.

sections.title: Reusing Connections and Pipelining Queries
sections.content:
Setting up a TCP connection generally costs one round trip. Clients and servers SHOULD support connection reuse so several DNS queries and responses can use one persistent connection. A client MUST NOT reuse the Message ID of a query that is still in flight on that connection.

To approach UDP performance, clients SHOULD pipeline queries instead of waiting for each response before sending the next query. DNS servers MUST expect pipelined queries, SHOULD process them concurrently, and SHOULD answer them all.

Clients MUST minimize concurrent connections and idle time. The RFC recommends no more than one connection for regular queries, one for zone transfers, and one per protocol layered on TCP. Servers are RECOMMENDED to use idle periods on the order of seconds, with no fixed value specified, and SHOULD reset the idle timer only after receiving a full DNS message.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a connection open avoids repeating its setup cost. A client can send several queries without waiting, but must match each reply correctly and avoid leaving idle connections open indefinitely.

sections.title: Matching Responses and Framing Messages
sections.content:
Authoritative servers and recursive resolvers are RECOMMENDED to prepare responses in parallel and send them as they become available, which may be out of order. Stub and recursive resolvers MUST handle responses arriving in a different order from their requests.

A client MUST match a response to an outstanding query on the same connection by Message ID. If the response has a question section, the client MUST also match QNAME, QCLASS, and QTYPE.

Each DNS message over TCP has a two-octet length field. Clients and servers SHOULD pass this field and its message to TCP together. A server MUST NOT close the connection merely because its first read did not contain the whole DNS message.
sections.plainLanguage: Replies can arrive in a different order from the questions, so clients match them using their identifiers and question details. The length field tells the receiver where each TCP message ends.

sections.title: TCP Fast Open
sections.content:
This section is non-normative. TCP Fast Open allows data in a SYN packet and can save up to one round trip when reopening a connection. A server supplies a cookie in its SYN-ACK, and a client can cache and reuse that cookie for later connections to the same server.

The RFC notes that DNS services using anycast may need servers behind load balancers to share a key so they create identical cookies for a client address. When TCP carries private DNS exchanges, implementers must ensure that data requiring protection is not accidentally sent in the clear.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP Fast Open can send data while a connection is being opened, using a cookie supplied by the server. The section is informative and highlights additional care for anycast and private DNS exchanges.

sections.title: Managing TCP Denial-of-Service Risks
sections.content:
The RFC recognizes concern that TCP can expose DNS servers to denial-of-service attacks. It recommends managing connections and request queues, and suggests configurable limits for total connections, connections per source, idle time, transactions per connection, and connection duration. It specifies no values for these limits.

Operators of recursive servers are advised to accept connections only from expected clients, such as through an access control list. This can help prevent unknown clients from exhausting connection limits.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP connections use server resources, so operators can limit their number and duration. Recursive servers can also restrict which clients may connect.
